title: Can the gaps between four arms change?
description: The four-arm figure from the book stays on the board while its arms are pulled apart to unequal gaps. A quarter turn then no longer puts each arm on the next, and the equal gaps are worked out from the full turn. The video ends with the paper windmill of the book, which has four equal blades.
teaching_notes: One idea: four identical arms with four angles of symmetry must share the full turn equally, so each gap is ninety degrees. Watch for students who think any four arms will do.

video_script.why: The child sees why four identical arms with four angles of symmetry must be equally spaced.
video_script.substitution: the book's four-arm figure, with the gaps between arms changed one at a time
video_script.anchor: the book's figure with four identical radial arms and a dot at its centre
video_script.payoff_line: The four arms cannot move; they stay equally spaced

final_answer.value: No: the four arms must stay 90° apart
final_answer.spoken: no, the four arms must stay ninety degrees apart

hold_back: No: the four arms must stay 90° apart
maths_rules: 4 identical arms with exactly 4 angles of symmetry: the smallest turn puts each arm on the next arm
so the 4 gaps between neighbouring arms are equal
the 4 gaps share the full turn: 360 ÷ 4 = 90
each gap is 90°, so the arms cannot be moved
unequal gaps give fewer angles of symmetry
video_script.design: The same four-arm figure with unequal gaps shown beside it. A quarter turn fails, then the gaps are made equal. The video ends with the paper windmill of the book as a real object with four equal blades.
open_questions: The book leaves this question open. The answer holds for four identical arms, as the worklist says.
